results.title: the platform audit log on the Management API
results.detail: 115 paths in the /v1 spec; 0 mention audit - the platform audit log has no read path, no export path and no delete path on the public API. It is Dashboard-only, which is why no tenant credential can rewrite it and also why nobody can pull it into a SIEM.

results.title: physical copies available on this project
results.detail: GET database/backups -> HTTP 200: pitr_enabled=false, walg_enabled=true, 1 logical backups listed, physical window none .. none. A fresh project has no history yet, which is itself the finding: the backstop only exists after the plan's first backup, and PITR is an add-on rather than a default.

results.title: restore levers on the Management API
results.detail: 6 backup paths: backups, backups/restore-pitr, backups/restore-point, backups/restore, backups/schedule, backups/undo. Any of them is reachable with the same PAT that can delete the audit rows, so the backstop is not protected from the actor it protects against - unless the restore lands in a DIFFERENT project (backup.restore_to_new_project in the entitlements A07 reads).

results.title: forging an audit entry GoTrue never wrote
results.detail: insert accepted; read back 1 row with a chosen actor (<email>), a chosen source IP and a created_at three days in the past. Removed afterwards: true. The table has no FK to auth.users and no trigger, so nothing reconciles a forged row against a real user.

results.title: rewriting an existing entry in place (source IP and action)
results.detail: UPDATE accepted: the row's source IP and its action were both rewritten (1 row now reads action=logout from 10.0.0.1). An audit row is a plain heap row - no immutability, no version, no updated_at to notice the edit by. Table left at 0 rows.

results.title: control: a DDL statement is findable in postgres_logs by its nonce
results.detail: create/drop table -> HTTP 201; the statement text appeared in postgres_logs 191s later. The search works and ingestion is live, so a miss below is a miss.

results.title: a bare DELETE on the audit table in postgres_logs
results.detail: delete -> HTTP 201; searched postgres_logs for its nonce for 191s: not found. log_statement=ddl does not cover DML, so the erasure of an audit row is not itself a logged statement.

results.title: a bare TRUNCATE on the audit table in postgres_logs
results.detail: truncate -> HTTP 201; searched for 191s: not found. TRUNCATE reads as DDL to a human and as `mod` to log_statement, so the fastest way to empty the table is also unlogged.

results.title: provenance on a statement the platform ran for you
results.detail: the control line is attributed to role=postgres, application_name=mgmt-api, and the platform appended a provenance comment naming the calling route and the acting identity (3 lines: -- source: POST /v1/projects/:ref/database/query -- user: pat:<id> -- date: 2026-09-08T05:40:26.577Z). Every tenant path - Dashboard, Management API, MCP - arrives as this one database role, so per-person attribution is not in Postgres.

results.title: log_statement through the Management API
results.detail: GET config/database/postgres -> HTTP 200, 0 keys, log_statement absent (log_connections absent). PUT log_statement=mod -> HTTP 400: {"message":": Unrecognized key: \"log_statement\""}. Statement-level DML logging is therefore a pgaudit job, not a config toggle.

results.title: pgaudit session mode catches the delete and the truncate
results.detail: create extension -> true; alter role postgres set pgaudit.log to 'write' -> true (rolconfig now pgaudit.log=write); no restart performed. DELETE -> HTTP 201: AUDIT line found 32s later. TRUNCATE -> HTTP 201: AUDIT line found 32s later. Both statements ran in sessions opened AFTER the ALTER ROLE, which is what makes a role-level GUC apply without a reboot.
results.evidence:
AUDIT: SESSION,1,1,WRITE,DELETE,,,"delete from auth.audit_log_entries where payload->>'action' = 'a04delueum02ln'

-- source: POST /v1/projects/:ref/database/query
-- user: pat:<id>
-- date: 2026-09-08T05:43:40.967Z",<not logged>
AUDIT: SESSION,1,1,WRITE,TRUNCATE TABLE,,,"-- a04trudjkj7cm1
truncate table auth.audit_log_entries

-- source: POST /v1/projects/:ref/database/query
-- user: pat:<id>
-- date: 2026-09-08T05:43:41.281Z",<not logged>

results.title: pgaudit object mode: audit this one table, log nothing else
results.detail: auditor role -> true; grant on the audit table -> true; pgaudit.role=a04_auditor -> true; pgaudit.log back to none -> true. DELETE -> HTTP 201: AUDIT line found 33s later (AUDIT: OBJECT,1,1,WRITE,DELETE,TABLE,auth.audit_log_entries,"delete from auth.audit_log_en). Object mode is the form worth running continuously - it says nothing about the other 99% of traffic.

results.title: log_connections through the API
results.detail: PUT log_connections=true -> HTTP 200; the session reports log_connections=off (a running session shows the value it started with, so the change lands for new connections). This is the lever that distinguishes a tenant path from a direct psql session, and it is off by default.

results.title: cleanup
results.detail: restored after the object phase: pgaudit not installed, postgres rolconfig pgaudit entries none, log_connections back to false.

results.title: audit-log keys in the documented auth config
results.detail: GET config/auth -> HTTP 200, 243 keys returned, 1 of them mention audit (audit_log_disable_postgres=true). audit_log_disable_postgres is present and reads true.

results.title: PATCH audit_log_disable_postgres through the Management API
results.detail: asked for audit_log_disable_postgres=false (the opposite of the true it held). PATCH -> HTTP 200; on re-read the key is true. A 2xx that leaves the value unchanged: the switch is accepted and ignored on the public API, so it is Dashboard-only (Authentication -> Configuration -> Audit Logs).

results.title: does a new auth event still reach the table
